A 53-year-old man is unable to direct eye movements voluntarily but has normal refl ex eye movements. A 37-year-old woman with fulminant liver failure and abnormal movements A 79-year-old gentleman with psychomotor slowness, memory loss and gradual intellectual decline Choose... Choose... Choose...
correctAnswer: A 53-year-old man is unable to direct eye movements voluntarily but has normal refl ex eye movements. → Progressive supranuclear palsy, A 37-year-old woman with fulminant liver failure and abnormal movements → Wilson's disease, A 79-year- old gentleman with psychomotor slowness, memory loss and gradual intellectual decline → Binswanger's disease
explanation:
1) Progressive supranuclear palsy- The most common early complaint is unsteadiness of gait and unexplained falling (retropulsion). It may take a year or longer for the characteristic syndrome-comprising supranuclear ophthalmoplegia, pseudo bulbar palsy, and axial dystonia to develop fully. Diffi culty in the voluntary vertical movement of the eyes (vertical gaze palsy). Bell's phenomenon (refl exive upturning of eyes on forced closure of the eyelids) and the ability to converge are also lost eventually, and the pupils then become small. 2) Wilson's disease- It is a rare autosomal recessive, progressive, but eminently treatable disorder of copper metabolism, causing a personality change, cognitive decline, and extrapyramidal disorder and cirrhosis of the liver. The extrapyramidal features include tremor, dysarthria, drooling, rigidity and bradykinesia. Kayser-Fleischer rings (copper deposits on Descemet's membrane of the cornea) are present in 95% of patients with neurological symptoms. 3) Progressive small vessel disease (Binswanger's disease)- This is subcortical dementia with a clinical course characterised by slow intellectual decline and generalised slowing. The clinical picture can be dominated by dementia, and there may be concomitant physical problems such as gait disorders or dysarthria. MRI scan shows small distinct infarcts (Lacunae) or more generalised white matter changes

(Leukoariasis). Depression and Pseudobulbar palsy are not uncommon.

stem: Epidemiological terms II Identify the most appropriate epidemiological term that refers to each of the following commonly used descriptions Risk of an illness Burden of disease Denominator of incidence density Denominator of prevalence Choose... Choose... Choose... Choose...
correctAnswer: Risk of an illness → Incidence, Burden of disease → Prevalence, Denominator of incidence density → Person-Years, Denominator of prevalence → Mid year population
explanation: In epidemiological terms, incidence is defi ned as the number of new cases of a disease in a population, divided by the total number of people at risk in the population per unit of time. Often when we refer to risk of a condition, we are talking about the incidence. This is also known as cumulative incidence or incidence rate. As not all those who are at risk can be followed up for long periods of time (due to attrition rate), a measure called incidence density which accounts for the varying time periods of follow up is often used in research. Although the numerator is the same as in the calculation of cumulative incidence, the denominator is now the sum of each individual's time at risk (Person-Years). In epidemiological terms, prevalence is defi ned as the number of existing cases of a disease in a population divided by total size of the population. Often when we refer to burden of a condition, we are talking about the prevalence.

explanation: Interpersonal psychotherapy may be particularly benefi cial for HIV patients with depressive symptoms. stem: Antipsychotic Drugs and Hyperglycemia in Older Patients With Diabetes Background: Evidence suggests that there is an association between antipsychotic drugs and new-onset diabetes, but little is known about the risk of hyperglycaemia among persons with pre-existing diabetes. Methods: Using population-based health databases in Ontario, Canada, persons aged 66 years or older with diabetes who started treatment with an antipsychotic drug from April 1, 2002, to March 31, 2006, were followed up from treatment start until March 31, 2007. The cohort was subdivided into 3 groups: insulin-treated, an oral hypoglycaemic agent only -treated, and no diabetes treatment. We defi ned cases as patients hospitalized (emergency department visit or hospital admissions) for hyperglycaemia. Each case was matched with up to 10 controls for age, sex, year of cohort entry and duration of follow-up. The authors compared the likelihood of hyperglycaemia among current users of atypical and typical antipsychotic agents with that among remote antipsychotic users (discontinued >180 days), based on prescriptions closest to the event date. Results: Of 13 817 patients studied, 1515 (11.0%) were hospitalized for hyperglycaemia. Current antipsychotic treatment was associated with a higher risk of hyperglycaemia compared with remote antipsychotic use in all diabetes treatment groups (overall adjusted rate ratio, 1.50; 95% confi dence interval, 1.29-1.74). The risk was increased among patients who were treated with atypical and typical antipsychotic agents and was extremely high among patients who were just starting treatment (only 1 prescription before event). Conclusions: Among older patients with diabetes, the initiation of treatment with antipsychotic drugs was associated with a signifi cantly increased risk of hospitalization for hyperglycaemia (P < .001). The risk was particularly high during the initial course of treatment and was increased with the use of all antipsychotic agents. Ref: Lipscombe et al., Arch Intern Med. 2009;169(14):1282-1289 What type of study is this?
explanation: This study uses a cohort of individuals to separate them into cases and controls based on an 'outcome' event. This is a nested case-control study.

stem: Which of the following is not a 'club drug'?
explanation: Club drugs are often associated with dance clubs and all-night parties (raves). These include LSD, gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB), ketamine, methamphetamine, and MDMA (ecstasy). GHB (Gamma hydroxyl butyrate),fl unitrazepam (a benzodiazepine) and ketamine are also called date rape drugs.

stem: Which treatment has been recommended by NICE as a treatment option in aiding abstinence from opioid misuse?
explanation: Naltrexone treatment has been found by NICE to be a cost eff ective treatment strategy in aiding abstinence from opioid misuse. It is recommended as a treatment option in detoxifi ed formerly opioid-dependent people who are highly motivated to remain in an abstinent programme. Close monitoring is important when Naltrexone treatment is initiated because of the higher risk of a fatal overdose at this time. An initial dose of 25 mg should be administered after a suitable opioid-free interval. Once the patient has tolerated this low Naloxone dose, subsequent doses can be increased to 50 mg daily as a maintenance dose. Naltrexone is a long-acting (72 hours) antagonist used to nullify eff ects of heroin if relapse occurs - thus preventing a 'lapse'becoming a relapse. Ref: NICE; Drug misuse, opioid detoxifi cation, Technology Appraisal 115

stem: A 25-year-old man is seen in the A&E unit with phencyclidine intoxication. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Benzodiazepines are helpful in managing aggression
Ataxia may occur at a later stage
explanation: Phencyclidine is a type of hallucinogen which has analgesic eff ects. PCP is usually smoked or snorted. It acts via sigma opioid and aspartate receptors as well as serotonergic eff ects. It can cause acute confusion, visual sensory distortions, aggression, and sudden severe violence. Psychosis is possible. PCP intoxication can cause disturbed co-ordination, vertical or horizontal nystagmus, numbness or diminished responsiveness to pain, ataxia and dysarthria with muscle rigidity. Pupil size is variable in PCP users, depending on the degree of hypoxia and intoxication.

stem: A 33-year-old man reveals that his 2-month-old son died of sudden infant death syndrome three years ago and ever since he has become increasingly preoccupied with protecting his family. He checks things six times and if unable to complete thefi fth time he becomes distressed, anxious and agitated. He also has a history of smoking heroin once every ten days to stop himself from becoming distressed. Which of the following is the most important component of treatment?
explanation: This gentleman presents with symptoms of OCD with compulsive rituals. Therefore, ritual prevention should be tried as a behavioural component of CBT in OCD treatment.

stem: Mrs. X has a history of opioid dependence and is still taking it. She is pregnant now and is willing to consider opioid detoxifi cation. This should be ideally done during
explanation: Women who are pregnant or planning a pregnancy should consider treatment with Methadone. Ideally, the mother should be encouraged to become abstinent prior to delivery-often this may not be possible. If pregnancy begins while a woman is taking high doses of methadone, the dosage should be reduced slowly (e.g., 1 mg every three days), and foetal monitoring must be carried out closely.If considering detoxifi cation, this should be done in the middle trimester - avoid fi rst trimester for the fear of abortion and last trimester for the fear of premature birth.

stem: An unemployed man presents to A&E with rigidity, tachycardia, hallucinations and sweating. His sister thinks that he has been using drugs lately. Which of the following is most likely?
explanation: Phencyclidine (PCP) or angel dust is not common in UK except as a contaminant of other drugs. PCP is usually smoked or snorted. Features of acute Hallucinogen Intoxication include marked anxiety or depression, paranoid ideation, perceptual changes, pupillary dilation, tachycardia, sweating, palpitations, tremors and incoordination. Also, PCP intoxication could cause the following additional features: vertical or horizontal nystagmus, numbness or diminished responsiveness to pain, ataxia and dysarthria with muscle rigidity.

stem: A patient with long-standing anxiety is managed by a GP. She was recently seen by her psychiatrist who made changes to her medications. She presents to the A&E with hallucinations of her joints being moved and nausea with agitation and anxiety. What is the diagnosis?
explanation: Symptoms of benzodiazepine withdrawal include autonomic hyperactivity, increased tremor, insomnia, nausea or vomiting, transient visual, tactile, or auditory hallucinations or illusions, psychomotor agitation and anxiety. Sometimes grand mal seizures can occur. Kinaesthetic hallucinations are characteristically related to benzodiazepine withdrawal and have been reported in some patients.

stem: What is the one year prevalence of clinical depression among those who have alcohol dependence?
explanation: The two main studies that have addressed the epidemiology of comorbidity are the National Comorbidity Survey (NCS) (Kessler et al. 1996) and the Epidemiologic Catchment Area (ECA) study (Regier et al. 1990). lmost one-third (29.2 percent) of NCS respondents with alcohol depeN-dence had a mood disorder. Alcohol- dependent respondents were 3.9 times more likely to have had major depressive disorder (27.9 percent) during the previ-ous year than those who were not alcohol dependent.

stem: The current prevalence of heroin use among adults in the UK is
explanation: The current prevalence of heroin use among adults in the UK is around 1% (male-to-female ratio of 2:1), with most treatment seekers being in their 20s.

stem: What percentage of those with alcohol withdrawal suff er from delirium tremens?
explanation: In most severe cases of alcohol withdrawal syndrome, delirium tremens may develop - this includes 5% of all cases. Delirium tremens is a toxic confusion state that occurs when alcohol withdrawal symptoms are severe and it is a life threatening state with mortality of approximately 5%. Disturbed autonomic functions (pulse, temperature and blood pressure changes on either direction), clouded consciousness with hallucinations (often Lilliputian) and agitation can occur.

stem: The percentage of men in the UK who drink excessively, above the recommended weekly limits for sensible drinking is
explanation: 27% of men and 15% of women in the UK drink excessively, above the recommended weekly limits for sensible drinking ONS, 1998). Up to 20% of patients presenting to general practice settings will be consuming alcohol at harmful or hazardous levels. Nearly 25% of UK household survey 2000 respondents had a hazardous pattern of drinking during the year before interview using the Alcohol Use Disorder Identifi cation Test (AUDIT score >= 8). The prevalence of hazardous drinking was higher among men (38%) than women (15%). This prevalence decreased with age. For women, prevalence was highest in the group aged from 16 to 19 years (32%), whereas for men the peak was found among those aged 20 to 24 (62%).

stem: The prevalence of alcohol related problems in a community is linked to the
options: Legal age limit for drinking alcohol
explanation: Total alcohol consumption is expressed by the 'per capita consumption'fi gure for persons over the age of 15. It is the average amount of pure alcohol (in litres) consumed in one year. It is calculated from the total amount of pure alcohol consumed in one year by the whole population (including children and abstainers), divided by the number of adults (in this case persons over the age of 15). The prevalence of alcohol related problems in a community is linked to Per capita alcohol consumption

stem: With regard to the epidemiology of addiction disorders in the UK, which of the following holds true?
options: 10% of cannabis users start using the drug below the age of 24
Cocaine is the most prevalent abused substance in the UK
1% of the adult population smoke cannabis regularly
2% of all school children used cannabis in the last year.
About 40% of users are below the age of 24
correctAnswer: About 40% of users are below the age of 24
explanation: Men (38%) are more than twice as likely to have any alcohol use disorder as women (16%). One in ten of 16 - 24 year olds used hard drugs in the last month. Cocaine is used by one and three quarter million young adults, but is less common than cannabis in the UK. 10% of the adult population smoke cannabis regularly. The highest numbers of drug users are amongst young adults under 25. 45% have used drugs at some point. Half of all cannabis users are under 24. 12% of all school children used cannabis in the last year. From Addicted Britain: State of the Nation report 2006.

stem: Which of the following is correct with regard to the epidemiology of alcohol use?
options: A large health burden is attributable to moderate drinkers
Conclusive evidence suggests light drinking is benefi
There is a trend of reducing home drinking
Most drinkers in the population are heavy users of alcohol
correctAnswer: A large health burden is attributable to moderate drinkers
explanation: Chronic heavy drinking (as with alcohol dependency) tends to cause longer-term health problems, whilst binge drinking (defi ned as consuming more than twice the daily recommended levels in one session) is more likely to increase the risk of acute health eff ects. Because moderate drinkers make up >50% of the alcohol users in the population, a large proportion of public health burden stems from this group. 70% of admissions to accident and emergency departments at peak times are alcohol-related. Home measures are often larger than pub measures - and as prices in licensed premises increase, and off -licence prices decrease, more people are drinking at home and therefore potentially drinking a lot more than they think. (from www.adph.org.uk)

stem: Mrs Dundheim comes to see you in clinic, accompanied by her adult daughter. You notice that there is some disturbance in her movements. Her daughter tells you that her mother's sister had Parkinson's Disease, and she's worried her mother might also have it. Which of the following physical signs is most indicative of Parkinson's disease?
explanation: A pill-rolling tremor, occurring at rest, is suggestive of Parkinson's disease, alongside bradykinesia, rigidity (both sides of the body, may start as unilateral rigidity), and mask-like facial appearance due to reduced facial expressions.

stem: The mental health liaison nurse has assessed a person presenting with suicidal ideas in the emergency department and asks you conduct a review. She is concerned that this person is at high risk. You look over her notes. What description of the patient is linked with the highest risk of suicide?
options: 32-year-old woman, married, subject to domestic violence
16-year-old woman, recently split up from boyfriend
explanation: Middle age, male gender, unemployment, with recent major loss are all signifi cant factors in contributing to the risk of suicide. This is made even higher by alcohol and/or drug misuse.

stem: Ben White is a 22-year-old student who attends A&E complaining of feeling out of touch with his body. He's not been able to sleep all night, he has stomach cramps, and on observation he's sweating profusely. He is worried it might be related to drug use. Which of the following clinical states in the best explanation?
explanation: These are typical features of withdrawal from opioids, also accompanied by piloerection, muscle spasms, and tremors.

stem: You are due to visit a 85 year old woman who lives alone, and who has for some months been complaining about her neighbour spying on her, listening to her movements through the walls, tapping on the walls when she's trying to sleep. Which if the following feature is most likely to be seen in persistent delusional disorder?
explanation: Persistent delusional disorder is often characterized by life long persistent non-bizarre delusions. The others are more suggestive of a broader psychotic illness, including schizophrenia.

stem: A 40-year-old man has had 5 depressive episodes in the past and every time following treatment of depression he had developed hypomania. What would you prescribe?
explanation: Antidepressant-induced mania/hypomania has been reported with all major antidepressant classes in a subgroup of about 20-40% of bipolar patients. Lithium may confer better protection against this outcome when compared with other standard mood stabilizers, although switch rates have been reported with comparable frequencies on or off mood stabilizers. Mood switches were less frequent in patients receiving lithium (15%) than in patients not treated with lithium (44%) in a small naturalistic study. Risk factors for antidepressant induced switch includes (i) previous antidepressant-induced manias, (ii) a bipolar family history, and (iii) exposure to multiple antidepressant trials and (iv) initial illness beginning in adolescence or young adulthood. Henry C, Sorbara F, Lacoste J, Gindre C, Leboyer M. Antidepressant- induced mania in bipolar patients: identifi cation of risk factors. J Clin Psychiatry 2001 Apr;62(4):249-55

stem: Which of the following has good evidence as an add-on therapy in partial responders with depression taking antidepressants?
explanation: The role of lithium as an augmenting agent is well established.

stem: Which of the following psychotropic medication is contraindicated during breastfeeding?
explanation: Lithium is contraindicated during breast-feeding ( Kohen, 2005) .However, "the use of lithium during breast feeding varies between absolute contraindication to mother's informed choice" (Maudsley Guidelines, 2007).Lithium serum concentration and CBC should be monitored for infants exposed to lithium. 40- 50% of maternal serum level is excreted in breast milk. Infant serum level can rise up to 200% of maternal serum concentration (range 5%-200%). Serum level in lithium can be raised due to diminished renal clearance in neonates. Toxicity has been reported -cyanosis, lethargy, Hypotonia, heart murmur ( these symptoms resolved after stopping the breast feeding)

stem: You started a patient severe depression on medications, and she is currently on 225 mg of venlafaxine and 45 mg of Mirtazapine. She has improved but developed a mixed aff ective state. What will you do?
options: Tell patient to take enough rest
explanation: Lithium has mood stabilizing properties, which are helpful in mixed aff ective states. Lithium will augment the eff ect of anti-depressants. But as mixed state must be managed in the same way as mania, we must discontinue the antidepressants, atleast the one with higher likelihood of switch; in this instance Venlafaxine.

stem: The sudden withdrawal of antiparkinsonian drugs could cause;
explanation: Levodopa preparations lead in the long term to the development of motor complications characterized by involuntary movements called dyskinesia andfl uctuations in the response to medication. Levodopa doses are maintained as low as possible while maintaining functionality. A former strategy to reduce motor complications was to withdraw patients from L-DOPA for some time. It is discouraged now since it can bring dangerous side eff ects such as neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Most people will eventually need levodopa and may develop residual motor complications Ref: Oxford handbook of medicine

stem: Which of the following is not a risk factor for puerperal psychosis?
explanation: Lack of social support is a risk factor for postnatal depression but not for puerperal psychosis.

stem: Which of the following is a common prescribed medication causing secondary mania?
explanation: L-Dopa and corticosteroids are the most common prescribed medications associated with secondary mania. Anabolic steroids, amantadine, bromocriptine, isoniazid, zidovudine and ephedrine (stimulant) can also cause secondary mania. In stimulant or other street drugs induced mania, if the mood state signifi cantly outlasts the drugged state then a diagnosis of bipolar disorder can be made.Evans DL, et al. Secondary mania: diagnosis and treatment. J Clin Psychiatry. 1995; 56:31-37.

stem: Which one of the following statements about Korasakoff 's syndrome is incorrect?
options: Confabulation and apathy are often prominent symptoms in the syndrome.
s syndrome is often associated with Wernicke's encephalopathy, which is the associated syndrome of confusion, ataxia, and
s syndrome is caused by thiamine defi
ciency, most commonly associated with chronic alcohol abuse.
Remote memory tends to be aff ected more than recent memory
s syndrome typically demonstrate a change in personality and these changes appear frontal lobe-like.
correctAnswer: Remote memory tends to be aff ected more than recent memory
explanation: Korsakoff s syndrome: Korsakoff s syndrome is an Amnestic syndrome caused by thiamine defi ciency, most commonly associated with chronic alcohol abuse. Other conditions such as prolonged starvation, gastric carcinoma, haemodialysis, hyperemesis gravidarum and gastric plication can also result in thiamine defi ciency. Korsakoff s syndrome is often associated with Wernicke's encephalopathy, which is the associated syndrome of confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia. Patients with Korsakoff s syndrome typically demonstrate a change in personality as well and these changes appear similar to the personality change ascribed to patients with frontal lobe lesions or degeneration. They tend to display a lack of initiative, diminished spontaneity, apathy and a lack of interest or concern. Recent memory tends to be aff ected more than is remote memory, but this feature is variable.

stem: Major depressive disorders are common in infarcts involving which part of the brain?
explanation: It was thought that left-hemisphere lesions produce more major or minor depression; this has been contested recently. Major depressive disorders are common in infarcts involving the basal ganglia, especially on the left hemisphere.

stem: A known bipolar patient relapses to a manic episode despite being on long-term mood stabiliser treatment with lithium. What will be thefi rst intervention?
explanation: It is sensible to check adequacy of lithium levels before planning other interventions.

stem: Jane is a 15-year-old girl currently admitted under the mental health act to an adolescent unit. She is having herfi rst episode of mania with psychotic features, having previously had a history of depression and been prescribedfl uoxetine. Which ONE of the following would be appropriate as a single agent in treatment of Jane's mania?
explanation: Recommendedfi rst line treatments for acute mania in children and adolescents include atypical antipsychotics such as aripiprazole, olanzapine, quetiapine and risperidone. Lithium can be used but would not be appropriate for Jane as a monotherapy as she has psychotic symptoms. Carbamazepine is not recommended. Sodium Valproate has not shown effi cacy in a small RCT for adolescent mania. (Reference: Taylor, D., Paton, C. and Kapur, S. (n.d.). Bipolar illness in children and adolescents. The Maudsley prescribing guidelines in psychiatry. 12th ed. Chichester: John Wiley & Sons, pp.364-365).

stem: James is a 17-year-old boy who was diagnosed with ADHD at the age of 8. He is seeing you in CAMHS and has asked about the neurobiological basis of his illness. He is aware the fronto-striatal network is implicated. Which brain region does NOT form part of the fronto-striatal network?
explanation: Data from neuroimaging, neuropsychology, neurochemistry and genetics consistently implicate the fronto-striatal network as a major contributor to the pathophysiology of ADHD. The network involves the lateral prefrontal cortex, the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, the caudate nucleus and putamen. The cerebellum is not part of the network. (Ref: Emond V, Joyal C, Poissant H. Structural and functional neuroanatomy of attention-defi cit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). L‘encéphale. 2009 Apr;35(2):107-14).

stem: Mr Neil Slater is a 16-year-old boy with a diagnosis of autistic spectrum disorder. He attends a special school and is soon to go to college. What is the likelihood that he would also have a diagnosis of epilepsy?
explanation: A recent study suggested that 22% of people with an autism spectrum disorder develop epilepsy by the age of 21 years. This is in keeping with previous studies. (Ref: Bolton PF, Carcani-Rathwell I, Hutton J, Goode S, Howlin P, Rutter M. Epilepsy in autism: features and correlates. The British Journal of Psychiatry. 2011 Apr;198(4):289-94.)

stem: Miss Joan Staff ord is a 15-year-old girl who has been suff ering from persistent low mood, reduced interest in activities, irritability, poor sleep and appetite, and diminishing school performance. She has had a trial of CBT which was not eff ective. Her parents are not willing for her to have any medications. Which of the following would be the most appropriate next step for her treatment?
explanation: NICE guidelines for treatment of depression in children and adolescents' states that if a trial of an initial psychological intervention is unsuccessful, an alternative, such of CBT, interpersonal therapy or family therapy should be considered. Fluoxetine can also be considered if the patient or carers are accepting of this. Repeating a therapy that has been ineff ective would not be helpful and counselling is unlikely to be successful if a formal psychotherapy has not worked. Individual psychotherapy and systemic family therapy are generally off ered after two trials of psychotherapy has been unsuccessful.

stem: Oliver is a 10-year-old boy who sustained a head injury falling from his skateboard 2 months ago. At the time he lost consciousness for less than 1 minute and had a GCS of 14 when he was later seen in A&E. He had some vomiting which settled within 24 hours of the injury. You are now seeing him 2 months later in CAMHS and his mother is wondering if there is a link between the head injury and his current complaint. Which ONE of the following neuropsychiatric syndromes or symptoms is NOT associated with mild Traumatic Brain Injury (mTBI) in children?
explanation: A systematic review found consistent associations between mTBI and ADHD, conduct disorder, depression and anxiety. However the review did suggest that the lack of pre-injury reports makefi rm conclusions diffi cult. Mania has not been reported. (Ref: Emery CA, Barlow KM, Brooks BL, Max JE, Villavicencio-Requis A, Gnanakumar V, Robertson HL, Schneider K, Yeates KO. A systematic review of psychiatric, psychological, and behavioural outcomes following mild traumatic brain injury in children and adolescents. The Canadian Journal of Psychiatry. 2016 May;61(5):259-69).

stem: Andrew Davies is a 9-year-old boy who has a diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder. His mother has noticed that sometimes he can comment on individual aspects of an object but not seem to see it as a ‘whole'. She gives the example of him being able to talk about wheels on a toy car but not being able to identify its overall shape. Which of the following best describes this phenomenon?
explanation: Central coherence theory underlies the central disturbance seen in people with autistic spectrum disorders. It is considered as a specifi c perceptual-cognitive style. It is loosely described as a limited ability to understand context or to "see the big picture".

stem: Jake is a 12-year-old boy with a diagnosis of conduct disorder. He has been assessed to have normal intelligence and does not have ADHD. His family have completed a course of multi-systemic therapy with a small benefi t. However, he continues to initiatefi ghts at school, has tortured the family dog and recently lit afi re in a rubbish bin outside his home. Which ONE of the following medications would be indicated?
explanation: Risperidone is licensed for the short-term management of severely aggressive behaviour in young people with conduct disorder who have not responded to psychosocial interventions. Quetiapine and olanzapine are not licensed. Atomoxetine or methylphenidate would be appropriate if he had ADHD but he does not have this diagnosis. (Ref: Antisocial behaviour and conduct disorders in children and young people: recognition and management. Clinical guideline [CG158] https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/CG158/chapter/1- Recommendations#pharmacological-interventions-2).

stem: During your CAMHS rotation you become interested in strategies to prevent depression in school age young people. You decide to join a local project which is off ering group training on coping strategies and mindfulness to all year 9 students, with additional 1:1 support for those who are identifi ed to have risk factors for depression. This is an example which of the following types of prevention?
explanation: This intervention targets all students (universal) and then students who are deemed to be at higher risk for developing depression (selective). Universal interventions target the general public or a whole population group. Selective interventions focus on a particular group or subgroup who have biological, psychological or social risk factors for developing a mental disorder. Indicated prevention targets high-risk individuals with detectable symptoms but whom do not yet meet the criteria for the disorder. (Ref: Weissberg RP, Kumpfer KL, Seligman ME. Prevention that works for children and youth: An introduction. American Psychological Association; 2003 Jun).

stem: Alan Davies is a 11-year-old who has just been diagnosed with ADHD and Tourette's in a local CAMHS clinic. Which of the following drugs should be prescribed for him in thefi rst instance?
explanation: It is generally recommended that alpha 2 adrenergic agonists, such as Clonidine, are usedfi rst-line in patients with ADHD and Tourette's. There is some evidence that stimulants, such as Methylphenidate, can increase the frequency and severity of tics. However, further evidence suggests that Methylphenidate can be well-tolerated in many patients, although Dexamphetamine is thought to signifi cantly worsen tics and should be avoided.

stem: Matthew Twist is a 17-year-old boy with a diagnosis of conduct disorder. He attends your clinic with his mother but just before you call them in, she asks to speak to you in private for a few moments. What is the best course of action?
options: Ask permission of the boy and speak to the mother if permitted
Deny the request and continue with the consultation
Insist that she speaks in front of her son
to sit in on the consultation
Speak to the mother and then continue with the consultation
correctAnswer: Ask permission of the boy and speak to the mother if permitted
explanation: Children older than 16 years of age can generally be assumed to have capacity to make decisions about their treatment and care and should be consulted regarding these matters. However, until they are 18 years, their parents can still consent on their behalf, although resolving situations like this may involve the courts. Realistically, most 16 and 17 year olds will consent to such a request.

stem: Tommy is 7 years old. His mother describes that life at home with him is very challenging: he is frequently not paying attention to her, he moves around the house very quickly, knocking things over, barging into her room without knocking. His teacher reports that at school he frequently interrupts her, cannot sit still in his chair and is so distracted he rarely manages tofi nish a piece of work. You consider starting him on medication for ADHD, but in taking a history you also discover he has an autoimmune liver disorder. Which of the following drugs is contraindicated in patients with ADHD and liver disease?
explanation: Atomoxetine is extensively metabolised in the liver by cytochrome P450 and associated with liver injury; its use is therefore contraindicated in patients with liver disease.

stem: You are working with a family in which one of the children has experienced sexual abuse. Which disorder is she most likely to develop in adulthood?
explanation: Personality Disorder is the adulthood diagnostic grouping with the highest relative risk in children who have experienced childhood sexual abuse. (BJPsych 2004, 184:416-421)

stem: Stella is a 15-year-old girl who has been losing weight over the preceding 9 months. Her mother reports that she counts the number of calories in her food, avoids eating with the rest of the family, and has taken to running several kilometres every day. What are the most important features of an initial assessment in clinic?
explanation: Measurement of weight and height, so as to work out the BMI, is crucial in the initially assessment as it will help to steer the direction of subsequent consultations, investigations and interventions. A BMI below 17.5 is a feature of anorexia nervosa.

stem: Natasha is a 19-year-old woman with a BMI of 15.8; she has been restricting her food intake for the past six months. She exercises daily in an eff ort to lose more weight. She believes she is overweight, despite evidence to the contrary. She does not wish to engage in talking therapy. You consider starting her on medication. Which of these would be the best initial option?
explanation: Pharmacological medication is not indicated as the sole treatment of anorexia nervosa. It may be used to treat co-morbid mental illness, such as depression, once the patient's weight has stabilised. Meta-analyses in the use of antipsychotics have failed to show effi cacy for body weight and other anorexia-related outcomes (J Clin Psychiatry 2012; 73(6):e757-66).

stem: Mr O'Mahony has had Parkinson's disease for 2 years and has now been diagnosed with Parkinson's dementia. He has recently started experiencing distressing visual hallucinations after having seen his neurologist last week. What would be thefi rst line management strategy for new psychotic symptoms in someone with Parkinson's dementia?
options: Review Parkinson's medications and consider reducing in consultation with neurologist
correctAnswer: Review Parkinson's medications and consider reducing in consultation with neurologist
explanation: The NICE guidelines for Parkinson's disease state that thefi rst course of action in new hallucinations is to reduce the dosage of any Parkinson's disease medicines that might have triggered hallucinations or delusions, taking into account the severity of symptoms and possible withdrawal eff ects. Seek advice from a healthcare professional with specialist expertise in Parkinson's disease before modifying therapy. Haloperidol is contraindicated in Parkinson's disease for its potential to worsen Parkinsonism and cause life threatening extra pyramidal side eff ects. Lithium is not indicated. Quetiapine may be considered if the symptoms are distressing and do not respond to other treatments. However, if Mr O'Mahony is not yet on a cholinesterase inhibitor this would the best medication to start prior to adding antipsychotics. (Ref: Parkinson's disease in adults. NICE guideline [NG71] Published date: July 2017.https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/Recommendations#pharmacological-management-of-non-motor-symptoms)

stem: Mrs Brenda Yung is a 82 year old woman with a diagnosis of mild Alzheimer' disease who wishes to remain in her home as long as possible. Her family is keen for her to move to a residential home. They are querying her capacity to make a decision around this. Which of the following is not true regarding mental capacity?
options: It can be enhanced by repeated discussions
It can only be assessed by a psychiatrist
It can vary and be present at sometimes and not at others
It may be impaired for one decision but not another
It applies to general decisions about every day issues
correctAnswer: It can only be assessed by a psychiatrist
explanation: Mental capacity does not have to be assessed by a psychiatrist. A wide variety of healthcare and legal professionals should be able to assess capacity, particularly with reference to their specifi c professional roles. Psychiatrists can be asked to assist if the decision is diffi cult or contentious.

stem: Dillan is 6 years old. His parents report that he has been found to have moderate learning diffi culties. He is rather socially anxious, makes poor eye contact, is prone to losing his temper quite easily. On examination he has large ears and a long face. What is the most likely genetic disorder?
explanation: Fragile X occurs in both genders but is more common in males than females; the FMR1 Gene is implicated, located on the X chromosome.

stem: Mark and Jenny's 26-month old daughter has been observed to lose many of the motor and verbal skills she had previously developed. For example, she is now unable to walk, her hands are making repeated movements seemingly without purpose, she no longer uses sentences in her speech. She has also begun to have seizures. Which of the following condition is this clinical picture highly suggestive of?
explanation: Retts Syndrome is a rare, non-inherited genetic postnatal neurological disorder that occurs almost exclusively in girls resulting in severe mental and physical disability, including due to seizures.

stem: Eva has a diagnosis of high functioning autism. She has a particular fascination with patterns in music and is able to perceive and describe complex reoccurring patterns. What description can be given to this particular talent?
explanation: Systematizing is the drive to analyse or construct systems and recognising repeating patterns in stimuli. This is a common feature of those with autistic spectrum disorders (see Philos Trans R Soc Lond B Biol Sci 2009; 364 (1522): 1377-1383)

stem: Mr David McDermott is a 40-year-old man with a diagnosis of DiGeorge syndrome. He has recently been referred to his local psychiatric clinic due to concerns about his mental health. Which of the following psychiatric disorders is most strongly associated with DiGeorge syndrome?
explanation: Schizophrenia is most strongly associated, with up to 30% of those with DiGeorge syndrome developing a psychotic illness.

stem: In your CAMHS clinic you are seeing Skye, a 3-year-old child with developmental delay. Her mother reports she had hypocalcaemia soon after she was born. Which ONE of the following syndromes are associated with neonatal hypocalcaemia?
explanation: In DiGeorge syndrome neonatal hypocalcaemia can result from hypoparathyroidism secondary to parathyroid aplasia or hypoplasia. The other disorders listed are not associated with neonatal hypocalcaemia. (References: Carpenter et al, 2017. Etiology of neonatal hypocalcaemia. https://www.uptodate.com/contents/etiology-of-hypocalcemia-in-infants-and-children)
